questions.stem: A tangent touches a circle at point T, and O is the centre. What is the size of the angle between the tangent and the radius OT?
questions.explanation: The tangent–radius theorem states that a tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact, so the angle is 90°. Choosing 45° confuses the tangent with a line that bisects a right angle, which no circle theorem produces. A tangent meeting a radius at 180° would mean the tangent passes through the centre, which is a diameter, not a tangent.

questions.stem: An angle at the centre of a circle standing on arc AB is 84°. What is the size of the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc, on the major arc side?
questions.explanation: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc, so the circumference angle is 84 ÷ 2 = 42°. Choosing 168° reverses the relationship and doubles instead of halves. Choosing 96° applies the cyclic quadrilateral supplementary rule, which does not relate a centre angle to a circumference angle.

questions.stem: A chord of a circle has a perpendicular drawn to it from the centre O. What does this perpendicular do to the chord?
options: It is equal in length to the chord.
It is equal in length to the radius.
questions.explanation: Joining the centre to each end of the chord creates two right-angled triangles sharing the perpendicular and with equal radii as hypotenuses, so they are congruent (RHS) and the two chord segments are equal — the perpendicular bisects the chord. Saying the perpendicular equals the radius is false: the radius is the hypotenuse, so it is always longer than the perpendicular. Trisecting is not a property produced by any circle theorem.

questions.stem: A chord of length 16 cm lies in a circle of radius 10 cm. How far is the chord from the centre?
questions.explanation: The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, giving a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 10 cm and one leg 8 cm, so the distance is √(100 − 64) = 6 cm. Choosing 8 cm uses the half-chord itself rather than the remaining leg. Choosing 2 cm subtracts the half-chord from the radius instead of using Pythagoras.

questions.stem: PA and PB are two tangents drawn to a circle with centre O from an external point P. If angle APB is 56°, what is the size of angle AOB?
questions.explanation: Angles OAP and OBP are each 90° by the tangent–radius theorem, so in quadrilateral OAPB the four angles sum to 360° and angle AOB = 360 − 90 − 90 − 56 = 124°. Choosing 112° doubles the angle at P as though it were an angle at the circumference standing on arc AB, but P is outside the circle, so that theorem does not apply. The cue is to look for the two right angles and use the angle sum of the quadrilateral.

questions.stem: A tangent touches a circle at A, and AB is a chord. The angle between the tangent and chord AB is 64°. Which statement correctly applies the alternate segment theorem?
options: Any angle subtended by AB in the alternate segment is 64°.
Any angle subtended by AB in the alternate segment is 26°.
The angle AOB at the centre is 64°.
Any angle subtended by AB in the same segment as the tangent angle is 64°.
questions.explanation: The alternate segment theorem states that the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle subtended by that chord in the alternate (opposite) segment, so that angle is 64°. Choosing 26° treats the tangent–chord angle as complementary to it, mixing in the 90° tangent–radius fact. Choosing the same segment reverses which segment the theorem names; the centre angle here would in fact be 128°, twice the tangent–chord angle.

questions.stem: Two tangents from an external point P touch a circle of radius 9 cm at A and B, and OP = 15 cm. What is the length of PA?
questions.explanation: Angle OAP is 90° because a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, so triangle OAP is right-angled at A with hypotenuse OP = 15; hence PA = √(225 − 81) = 12 cm. The answer √306 adds the squares instead of subtracting, treating PA as the hypotenuse rather than OP. The cue is that the line from the external point to the centre is always the hypotenuse, since the right angle sits at the point of contact.

questions.stem: AB is a diameter of a circle with centre O, and C is another point on the circle. If angle CAB = 34°, what is the size of angle ABC?
options: 146°, because angle ABC and angle CAB are supplementary
56°, because angle ACB is 90° and the angles of triangle ABC sum to 180°
68°, because the angle at the circumference is double the angle at the centre
34°, because triangle ABC is isosceles with AC = BC
questions.explanation: An angle at the circumference standing on a diameter is a right angle, so angle ACB = 90°; the three angles of triangle ABC must total 180°, giving 180° − 90° − 34° = 56°. The option giving 68° reverses the centre–circumference relationship (the angle at the centre is double the angle at the circumference, and in any case that rule is not what is needed here). The cue is the word 'diameter': it immediately fixes the third vertex angle at 90°, turning the problem into simple angle-sum work in a right-angled triangle.

questions.stem: For a triangle with sides a, b and c, and angles A, B and C opposite those sides, the cosine rule is correctly written as:
questions.explanation: The cosine rule links the three sides to one angle, and that angle must be the one opposite the side being squared on the left, giving a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A. The version with + 2bc cos A is tempting because it looks like Pythagoras with an extra piece, but the subtraction is essential: when A is acute, cos A is positive and a² must be less than b² + c². Pairing side a with cos C is the other common slip — always check that the single squared side on the left sits opposite the angle inside the cosine.

questions.stem: Which statement is the sine rule for a triangle ABC?
options: a sin A = b sin B = c sin C
a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C
a/sin B = b/sin C = c/sin A
a/sin A = b/sin B = sin C/c
questions.explanation: The sine rule states that each side divided by the sine of the angle opposite it gives the same ratio, so a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. The version a/sin B = b/sin C = c/sin A pairs each side with the wrong angle — the pairing must always be side-with-opposite-angle. Note that flipping every term to sin A/a = sin B/b = sin C/c is also valid, but a form that flips only one term, or that multiplies instead of divides, is not.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, sides a and b are known along with the angle C between them. The area rule gives the area as:
questions.explanation: The area rule comes from Area = ½ × base × height, where the height is a sin C, giving Area = ½ab sin C — the sine of the angle included between the two known sides. The option ½ab cos C is tempting because cosine appears in the cosine rule, but cosine gives a horizontal projection, not the perpendicular height. The cue is 'included angle with sine': the angle used must sit between the two sides you multiply.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, b = 7 cm, c = 9 cm and the angle A between them is 40°. Correct to one decimal place, how long is side a?
questions.explanation: Using a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A gives a² = 49 + 81 − 2(7)(9)cos 40° = 130 − 126 × 0.7660 ≈ 33.5, so a ≈ 5.8 cm. The answer 11.4 cm comes from using √(49 + 81), that is, treating the triangle as right-angled and dropping the cosine term altogether; 15.0 cm comes from adding rather than subtracting that term. A useful check: side a is opposite the smallest angle here, so it should be shorter than both 7 cm and 9 cm.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, angle A = 35°, angle B = 80° and side a = 12 cm. Correct to one decimal place, how long is side b?
questions.explanation: By the sine rule, b = a sin B / sin A = 12 × sin 80° ÷ sin 35° ≈ 11.82 ÷ 0.5736 ≈ 20.6 cm. The value 7.0 cm comes from inverting the ratio (using 12 × sin 35° ÷ sin 80°), which would wrongly make the side opposite the larger angle the shorter one. Check plausibility: angle B is larger than angle A, so b must be longer than 12 cm.

questions.stem: A triangular garden bed has two sides of 8 m and 11 m with an angle of 52° between them. Correct to one decimal place, what is its area?
questions.explanation: The area rule gives Area = ½ × 8 × 11 × sin 52° = 44 × 0.7880 ≈ 34.7 m². The answer 27.1 m² uses cos 52° instead of sin 52°, which does not give the perpendicular height; 44.0 m² ignores the angle entirely, which would only be correct if the included angle were 90°. Since sin 52° is less than 1, the true area must be smaller than 44 m².

questions.stem: A triangle has sides of 5 cm, 7 cm and 10 cm. Correct to one decimal place, what is the size of its largest angle?
questions.explanation: The largest angle lies opposite the longest side, so use 10² = 5² + 7² − 2(5)(7)cos θ, giving cos θ = (25 + 49 − 100) ÷ 70 = −0.3714 and θ ≈ 111.8°. The answer 68.2° comes from ignoring the negative sign on the cosine; a negative cosine is the signal that the angle is obtuse, so discarding the sign always loses the obtuse solution. The answers 40.5° and 27.7° are the angles opposite the 7 cm and 10 cm... in fact opposite the 7 cm and 5 cm sides, so they cannot be the largest.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, a = 9 cm, b = 12 cm and angle A = 40°. The sine rule gives sin B ≈ 0.857. Which statement about angle B is correct?
options: B could be about 59.0° or about 149.0°, since sines repeat every 90°
B must be about 31.0°, because B is found by taking 90° minus the inverse sine
B could be about 59.0° or about 121.0°, since both leave a positive angle C
B must be about 59.0°, because the inverse sine on a calculator gives only that value
questions.explanation: Because sin(180° − x) = sin x, an unknown angle found from its sine has two candidates, here about 59.0° and 180° − 59.0° = 121.0°; both are possible since 40° + 121.0° is still less than 180°, so this is the ambiguous case. Saying B must be 59.0° because that is what the calculator returns is the most common error — the calculator only ever returns the acute value, so you must test the obtuse supplement yourself. The obtuse candidate is 180° minus the acute one, not 180° − 31° or a shift of 90°.

questions.stem: A point P lies on the unit circle so that the ray from the origin to P makes an angle of x with the positive x-axis, measured anticlockwise. The coordinates of P are:
questions.explanation: On a circle of radius 1 the horizontal displacement of P is cos x and the vertical displacement is sin x, so P = (cos x, sin x); this is exactly how the functions are defined for any real x. The reversed pair (sin x, cos x) is the most common slip — it comes from remembering the letters but not which axis each belongs to. Cue: cosine goes with the x-axis (both come first, alphabetically and on the coordinate pair).

questions.stem: Using the unit circle definition, the range of the function y = sin(x) for real values of x is:
questions.explanation: The value of sin(x) is the y-coordinate of a point on a circle of radius 1, so it can be as low as -1 and as high as 1, and both endpoints are actually reached (at 270° and 90°). Choosing 0 ≤ y ≤ 1 comes from only picturing the first quadrant of the circle, where the y-coordinate is never negative. Remember that x runs over all real numbers (the domain), while the output is trapped between -1 and 1.

questions.stem: What is the period of the graph of y = tan(x)?
questions.explanation: Because tan(x) = sin(x)/cos(x), a rotation of 180° on the unit circle sends the point (cos x, sin x) to (-cos x, -sin x), and the two sign changes cancel in the ratio, so the graph repeats every 180°. The answer 360° is tempting because that is the period of both sine and cosine, but tangent completes a full cycle in half that interval. Cue: the tangent graph has a branch between each pair of asymptotes, and the asymptotes are 180° apart.

questions.stem: The graph of y = tan(x) has vertical asymptotes at x = 90°, 270°, 450°, and so on. On the unit circle, this happens because at these angles:
options: cos(x) = 0, so the ratio sin(x)/cos(x) is undefined
sin(x) = 0, so the ratio sin(x)/cos(x) is undefined
both sin(x) and cos(x) equal 1, so the ratio is too large
the point on the unit circle leaves the circle entirely
questions.explanation: Tangent is defined as sin(x)/cos(x), so it is undefined exactly where the x-coordinate on the unit circle is zero, which occurs at 90°, 270° and every 180° after that. The option naming sin(x) = 0 confuses the zeros with the asymptotes: where sin(x) = 0 (at 0°, 180°, 360°) the tangent graph crosses the axis rather than blowing up. Cue: a zero denominator gives an asymptote, a zero numerator gives an x-intercept.

questions.stem: Using the unit circle, the exact value of sin(150°) is:
questions.explanation: An angle of 150° lands in the second quadrant, where the y-coordinate is positive, and its related first-quadrant angle is 180° - 150° = 30°, so sin(150°) = sin(30°) = 1/2. The value √3/2 comes from using 60° as the related angle instead of 30°, which happens if you subtract from 90° rather than 180°. Cue: for a second-quadrant angle, the related acute angle is 180° minus the angle, and sine stays positive there.

questions.stem: Comparing the graphs of y = sin(x) and y = cos(x) over 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°, which statement is correct?
options: The cosine graph has twice the period of the sine graph.
The cosine graph is the sine graph translated 90° to the left.
The cosine graph is the sine graph translated 180° to the left.
The cosine graph is the sine graph reflected in the x-axis.
questions.explanation: Since cos(x) = sin(x + 90°), every point of the sine graph moves 90° in the negative x-direction to give the cosine graph; you can see this because cosine peaks at 0° while sine peaks at 90°. The 180° translation is wrong: shifting sine by 180° produces -sin(x), not cosine. Cue: compare where each graph reaches its maximum — the gap between those maxima is the size of the shift.

questions.stem: For 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°, the equation sin(x) = -1/2 is satisfied by which pair of values?
questions.explanation: The y-coordinate on the unit circle is negative in the third and fourth quadrants, and the related acute angle is 30° because sin(30°) = 1/2, giving x = 180° + 30° = 210° and x = 360° - 30° = 330°. The pair 150° and 210° mixes one second-quadrant solution (where sine is positive) with one correct third-quadrant solution. Cue: a negative sine means both answers must come from below the x-axis, so both lie between 180° and 360°.

questions.stem: On the unit circle, a point P is at an angle x from the positive x-axis. The value of tan(x) can be interpreted as:
options: the distance from the origin to P along the radius
the length of arc from the positive x-axis around to P
the gradient of the line through the origin and P
the vertical distance from P to the x-axis
questions.explanation: The line through the origin and P rises sin(x) for a run of cos(x), so its gradient is sin(x)/cos(x) = tan(x); this also explains why tan(x) is undefined when the line is vertical. The vertical distance from P to the x-axis is sin(x), not tan(x), which is the most common mix-up. Cue: tangent is a ratio of two coordinates, so it measures steepness rather than any single length.

questions.stem: Solve sin(x) = 1/2 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.
questions.explanation: The first-quadrant solution is x = 30°, and sine is also positive in the second quadrant, where the solution is 180° − 30° = 150°. The pair 30° and 210° comes from using 180° + 30°, which is the rule for a negative sine value, not a positive one. Cue: positive sine means quadrants 1 and 2, so subtract the reference angle from 180°; the pair 60° and 120° wrongly treats 60° as the reference angle for a value of 1/2.

questions.stem: Solve tan(x) = 1 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.
questions.explanation: Tangent is positive in the first and third quadrants, and it repeats every 180°, so from x = 45° the second solution is 45° + 180° = 225°. The pair 45° and 135° uses the 180° − x rule, which belongs to sine, and 135° actually gives tan = −1. Cue: for tangent equations, add 180° to get the next solution rather than reflecting about 180°.

questions.stem: How many solutions does the equation sin(x) = 1.4 have for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°?
options: Two solutions, one in each of the first two quadrants
Four solutions, one in each of the four quadrants
No solutions, because sine values never exceed 1
One solution, found by taking the inverse sine of 1.4
questions.explanation: On the unit circle sin(x) is the y-coordinate of a point on a circle of radius 1, so it always lies between −1 and 1; a value of 1.4 is impossible. The option claiming one solution from the inverse sine is wrong because a calculator returns an error for sin⁻¹(1.4) — no angle produces that value. Cue: before solving, check the required value lies within −1 ≤ sin(x) ≤ 1.

questions.stem: Solve 2cos(x) + 1 = 0 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.
questions.explanation: Rearranging gives cos(x) = −1/2, with reference angle 60°; cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants, giving 180° − 60° = 120° and 180° + 60° = 240°. The pair 60° and 300° solves cos(x) = +1/2, which comes from dropping the negative sign when rearranging. Cue: isolate cos(x) first, then let its sign decide which quadrants to use.

questions.stem: A calculator gives sin⁻¹(0.4) ≈ 23.6°. What is the other solution of sin(x) = 0.4 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°, correct to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: Sine is positive in the first and second quadrants, so the second solution is 180° − 23.6° = 156.4°. The answer 203.6° uses 180° + 23.6°, which gives a point in the third quadrant where sine is negative. Cue: check the sign of the sine value, then pick the quadrant pair before applying the reference angle.

questions.stem: Solve tan(x) = −√3 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.
questions.explanation: Since tan(60°) = √3, the reference angle is 60°, and tangent is negative in the second and fourth quadrants: 180° − 60° = 120° and 360° − 60° = 300°. The pair 60° and 240° solves tan(x) = +√3, ignoring the negative sign. Cue: √3 belongs to 60° while 1/√3 belongs to 30°, and a negative tangent sends you to quadrants 2 and 4.

questions.stem: Solve sin(2x) = 1/2 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.
questions.explanation: If 0° ≤ x ≤ 360° then 0° ≤ 2x ≤ 720°, so 2x = 30°, 150°, 390° or 510°, and halving each gives 15°, 75°, 195° and 255°. Listing only 15° and 75° forgets to extend the range for 2x, so the two extra solutions from the second revolution are lost. The list 30°, 150°, 390°, 510° gives values of 2x rather than of x. Cue: double the interval, solve for 2x, then halve every answer.

questions.stem: Solve cos(x) = −0.7 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°, giving answers correct to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: The reference angle is cos⁻¹(0.7) ≈ 45.6°, and cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants, giving 180° − 45.6° = 134.4° and 180° + 45.6° = 225.6°. The pair 45.6° and 314.4° solves cos(x) = +0.7, ignoring the negative sign. Cue: take the inverse cosine of the size of the number to get the reference angle, then let the sign choose the quadrants.

questions.stem: A rectangular prism has length l, width w and height h. The length of its space diagonal (from one corner to the opposite corner) is:
questions.explanation: Pythagoras is applied twice: the base diagonal is √(l² + w²), then the space diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs √(l² + w²) and h, giving √(l² + w² + h²). The tempting choice 'l² + w² + h²' is the square of the diagonal — the square root has been forgotten. Also note that '√(l² + w²) + h' wrongly adds the height on as a straight length instead of treating it as a perpendicular leg.

questions.stem: A rectangular box measures 3 cm by 4 cm by 12 cm. How long is its longest diagonal?
questions.explanation: The space diagonal is √(3² + 4² + 12²) = √(9 + 16 + 144) = √169 = 13 cm. The answer '5 cm' is only the diagonal of the 3 cm by 4 cm face, not the full space diagonal, and '169 cm' is the value before taking the square root. The cue is that the longest diagonal must use all three dimensions and end with a square root.

questions.stem: In a rectangular prism, the angle that a space diagonal makes with the base is found from a right-angled triangle in which:
options: the side opposite the angle is the vertical edge and the adjacent side is the base diagonal
the side opposite the angle is the base diagonal and the adjacent side is the vertical edge
the side opposite the angle is the vertical edge and the adjacent side is the longest base edge
the side opposite the angle is the base diagonal and the hypotenuse is the vertical edge
questions.explanation: The angle sits at the base corner between the space diagonal and the base diagonal, so the base diagonal is adjacent, the vertical edge is opposite, and the space diagonal is the hypotenuse. Swapping them, as in 'the base diagonal is opposite and the vertical edge is adjacent', describes the angle at the top of the prism instead. The cue is to draw the vertical triangle first and mark the angle at the corner on the base.

questions.stem: A rectangular prism has a base measuring 6 cm by 8 cm and a height of 5 cm. Correct to one decimal place, what angle does a space diagonal make with the base?
questions.explanation: The base diagonal is √(6² + 8²) = 10 cm, so tan θ = 5/10 = 0.5 and θ ≈ 26.6°. The answer '30.0°' comes from using sin θ = 5/10, but 10 cm is the horizontal side, not the hypotenuse, so tangent is required. Check which two sides you actually know before choosing the ratio: two legs means tangent.

questions.stem: A right square pyramid has a base of side 10 cm and a vertical height of 12 cm. What is the slant height from the apex to the midpoint of a base edge?
questions.explanation: The right triangle is formed by the vertical height 12 cm, the horizontal distance from the centre of the base to the midpoint of an edge (half of 10, so 5 cm), and the slant height: √(12² + 5²) = 13 cm. The value '13.9 cm' uses half the base diagonal (about 7.07 cm) and so gives the length of a slanting lateral edge to a corner, not the slant height to an edge midpoint. Decide first whether the foot of your triangle lands on an edge midpoint (use half the side) or a corner (use half the diagonal).

questions.stem: A storage room is 8 m long, 6 m wide and 3 m high. Correct to one decimal place, what is the length of the longest straight rod that can fit inside?
questions.explanation: The longest rod lies along the space diagonal: √(8² + 6² + 3²) = √109 ≈ 10.4 m. The answer '10.0 m' is only the floor diagonal √(8² + 6²), which ignores the height, while '13.0 m' adds the 3 m height onto that floor diagonal instead of using Pythagoras again. The cue is that a genuinely three-dimensional length uses all three measurements inside one square root.

questions.stem: In a cube, two face diagonals are drawn from the same vertex on two different faces, and their far ends are joined. What is the size of the angle between those two face diagonals at that vertex?
questions.explanation: All three sides of the triangle formed are face diagonals of the same cube, so they are equal in length, making the triangle equilateral and each angle 60°. The answer '45°' is the angle a face diagonal makes with an edge of its own face, which is a different angle in the same cube. Whenever the joining segment is also a face diagonal, look for the equilateral triangle rather than reaching for a trigonometric ratio.

questions.stem: A rectangular prism measures 4 cm by 3 cm by 12 cm. Correct to one decimal place, what angle does the space diagonal make with the 4 cm by 12 cm face?
questions.explanation: Project the diagonal onto the 4 by 12 face: that projection is √(4² + 12²) = √160 ≈ 12.649 cm, and the perpendicular distance to the face is the remaining dimension, 3 cm, so tan θ = 3/12.649 and θ ≈ 13.3°. The answer '14.0°' comes from using tan θ = 3/12, using an edge of the face rather than the face diagonal as the horizontal side. Always use the projection of the diagonal onto the face, which is that face's diagonal.

questions.stem: In the context of solving a spatial problem, an algorithm is best described as:
options: a reasonable estimate of the answer that is checked afterwards against the drawn figure
a finite, ordered sequence of unambiguous steps that produces the solution whenever it is followed
a single formula that is substituted into once to produce the solution for that shape
a carefully drawn scale diagram from which the required lengths and angles are measured
questions.explanation: An algorithm is a finite set of clearly defined steps in a fixed order that anyone (or a computer) can follow to reach the same solution, which is why it can be tested and refined. Calling it 'a single formula that is substituted into once' confuses one calculation step with the whole procedure — an algorithm may contain several formulas, decisions and repeats. The cue is the words 'steps' and 'order': algorithms are procedures, not single results.

questions.stem: After testing an algorithm on several shapes, 'refining' it means:
options: redrawing the diagrams neatly so each step is easier for a reader to follow
running exactly the same steps again more carefully, hoping to avoid arithmetic slips
reporting only the shapes where it worked and leaving out the failures
altering or adding steps so failed cases now work, or so it runs more efficiently
questions.explanation: Refinement is a change to the procedure itself, prompted by what testing revealed: extra conditions, reordered steps, or a more efficient method. 'Running exactly the same steps again more carefully' fixes a calculation error, not the algorithm, so the same failures would reappear. Ask yourself whether the instructions changed — if not, no refining has happened.

questions.stem: An algorithm estimates the area of an irregular leaf by placing it on 1 cm grid paper: count squares fully inside the outline, add half of the number of squares only partly covered. The leaf covers 46 full squares and 12 partly covered squares. What area does the algorithm output?
questions.explanation: Following the steps exactly: 46 full squares plus half of 12 partial squares gives 46 + 6 = 52 cm². Choosing 58 cm² counts every partial square as a whole square, which is a different (and less accurate) algorithm, while 46 cm² ignores the partial squares altogether. Read the counting rule carefully before adding — the 'half' step is what makes this estimate reasonable.

questions.stem: An algorithm must decide whether a point (x, y) lies inside a circle centred at the origin with radius r. Which test should the decision step use?
options: Inside if x² + y² is less than r
Inside if x + y is less than r
Inside if the square root of (x² + y²) is greater than r
Inside if x² + y² is less than r²
questions.explanation: The distance from the origin to (x, y) is √(x² + y²), so the point is inside when that distance is less than r, which is equivalent to x² + y² < r² and avoids computing a square root. 'Inside if x² + y² is less than r' compares a squared distance with an unsquared radius, so the units do not match and the test fails (for example (0.9, 0) with r = 0.5). Square both sides of a distance comparison, or neither.

questions.stem: A rectangular floor is 240 cm by 180 cm. An algorithm repeatedly subtracts the smaller measurement from the larger until the two are equal, then uses that value as the tile side. What does it output for the largest identical square tiles that cover the floor with no cutting?
options: Tiles of side 60 cm, needing 12 tiles
Tiles of side 30 cm, needing 48 tiles
Tiles of side 90 cm, needing 6 tiles
Tiles of side 180 cm, needing 2 tiles
questions.explanation: Repeated subtraction gives 240 − 180 = 60, then 180 − 60 = 120, 120 − 60 = 60, so the process stops at 60, the highest common factor of 240 and 180; the floor holds 4 by 3 = 12 such tiles. Tiles of side 30 cm do fit exactly, but 30 is not the largest possible side, so the algorithm's stopping value has been misread. Tiles of 90 cm or 180 cm do not divide 240, so they would require cutting.

questions.stem: An algorithm for tiling reads: (1) divide the wall length by the tile side; (2) divide the wall height by the tile side; (3) multiply the two results. For a wall 3.6 m by 2.4 m tiled with 30 cm square tiles, what does the algorithm output?
questions.explanation: Converting to the same units, 3.6 m ÷ 0.3 m = 12 and 2.4 m ÷ 0.3 m = 8, so step 3 gives 12 × 8 = 96 tiles. The answer 28.8 comes from dividing the wall area (8.64 m²) by the tile side length rather than following the algorithm's steps, which mixes units of area and length. Follow the steps exactly as written, and check that both dimensions are converted before dividing.

questions.stem: An algorithm classifies a triangle from three side lengths a, b, c: let h be the largest; if h² = (sum of the squares of the other two) output 'right', if h² is greater output 'obtuse', otherwise output 'acute'. Which test case exposes a flaw in this algorithm?
options: 5, 5, 5 — the algorithm cannot compare squares when all three sides are equal in length
2, 3, 9 — the algorithm outputs 'obtuse' even though these lengths cannot form a triangle at all
3, 4, 6 — the algorithm outputs 'obtuse' when this set of lengths actually forms an acute triangle
6, 8, 10 — the algorithm outputs 'right' when a triangle with three different sides must be scalene
questions.explanation: The algorithm never checks the triangle inequality, so an input like 2, 3, 9 (where 9 > 2 + 3) is accepted and labelled 'obtuse' although no such triangle exists; adding a validity check is the refinement needed. The option using 3, 4, 6 looks like the same kind of flaw, but 36 > 9 + 16 means that triangle genuinely is obtuse, so the output is correct there. Test for missing input checks first: ask whether the algorithm would notice an impossible set of lengths.

questions.stem: A student designs this algorithm to decide whether two triangles are similar: measure the largest angle in each triangle; if the two largest angles are equal, output 'similar', otherwise output 'not similar'. Which test case exposes a flaw in the algorithm?
options: A triangle with sides 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm and a triangle with sides 6 cm, 8 cm, 10 cm
An equilateral triangle of side 4 cm and an equilateral triangle of side 9 cm
A triangle with angles 100°, 50°, 30° and a triangle with angles 100°, 60°, 20°
A triangle with angles 80°, 60°, 40° and a larger triangle with angles 80°, 60°, 40°
questions.explanation: Similarity needs all pairs of corresponding angles equal, so matching only the largest angle is not enough: 100°, 50°, 30° and 100°, 60°, 20° share their largest angle but the other angles differ, so the algorithm wrongly outputs 'similar' and the flaw is revealed. The 3-4-5 and 6-8-10 pair is tempting because it looks like a scaling test, but those triangles really are similar (both have a 90° largest angle), so the algorithm's output is correct and nothing is exposed. The same applies to the two equilateral triangles and to the 80°-60°-40° pair: a valid test of a faulty step must be a case where the algorithm gives the wrong answer, not one where it happens to agree.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a valid test for proving two triangles congruent?
options: A right angle, the hypotenuse and one other side equal (RHS)
Two sides and a non-included angle equal (SSA)
Two sides and the included angle equal (SAS)
Two angles and a corresponding side equal (AAS)
questions.explanation: SSA is not a congruence test because two sides and an angle that is not between them can produce two genuinely different triangles (the ambiguous case), so the data does not fix the shape. SAS is the closely related test that is valid — the difference is that the known angle sits between the two known sides, which locks the third side. AAS and RHS are both standard valid tests. Cue: check whether the angle is included between the two given sides.

questions.stem: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral (all four vertices on one circle). If angle A = 85°, what is angle C?
questions.explanation: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, so angle C = 180° − 85° = 95°. Choosing 85° comes from assuming opposite angles are equal, which is a property of parallelograms, not of cyclic quadrilaterals. Cue: for points on a circle, opposite angles add to 180°, not match each other.

questions.stem: P and Q are points on a circle with centre O, and R is another point on the major arc. If angle POQ = 130°, what is angle PRQ?
questions.explanation: The angle at the centre standing on an arc is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc, so angle PRQ = 130° ÷ 2 = 65°. The answer 260° reverses the theorem by doubling the central angle instead of halving it. Cue: the angle at the centre is always the larger of the pair.

questions.stem: To prove that the diagonals of parallelogram ABCD bisect each other at O, which pair of congruent triangles and which test should be used?
options: Triangles AOB and COD by AAS, using alternate angles on the parallel sides and AB = DC
Triangles AOB and COD by SSS, using AO = OC, BO = OD and AB = DC
Triangles AOB and COD by SAS, using AO = OC, BO = OD and the vertically opposite angles at O
Triangles AOB and BOC by RHS, using the right angle at O and the shared side OB
questions.explanation: The known facts are that opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal and parallel, so AB = DC and the alternate angles at A and C, and at B and D, are equal — that is AAS, and the congruence then gives AO = OC and BO = OD. The SSS and SAS options both assume AO = OC and BO = OD, which is exactly the result being proved, so they argue in a circle. Cue: a proof may never use its own conclusion as a given.

questions.stem: Two chords of a circle, AB and CD, cross at an interior point P. If AP = 4 cm, PB = 9 cm and CP = 6 cm, what is PD?
questions.explanation: For chords meeting inside a circle, AP × PB = CP × PD, so 4 × 9 = 36 and PD = 36 ÷ 6 = 6 cm. Choosing 7 cm comes from treating the relationship as additive (4 + 9 = 6 + PD) instead of multiplicative. Cue: the intersecting chords result comes from similar triangles, so it compares products of lengths, not sums.

questions.stem: AB is a diameter of a circle with centre O, and C is any other point on the circle. What can be deduced about angle ACB?
options: It is half of angle CAB, wherever C is placed
It equals angle AOB, the angle at the centre O
It grows larger as C moves closer to the diameter AB
It is 90°, wherever C is placed on the circle
questions.explanation: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc; since AB is a diameter the central angle AOB is a straight angle of 180°, so the angle at C is always 90°. The claim that angle ACB equals angle AOB confuses the angle at the circumference with the angle at the centre — those are in a 1:2 ratio, not equal. The cue is the word 'diameter': it forces the central angle to be 180°, so the inscribed angle is fixed at 90° and does not depend on where C sits.

questions.stem: A tangent touches a circle at A, and AB is a chord. The angle between the tangent and the chord AB is 62°. Point C lies on the major arc, in the alternate segment. What is the size of angle ACB?
questions.explanation: By the alternate segment theorem, the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment, so angle ACB is 62°. The tempting answer 28° comes from subtracting from 90°, using the tangent–radius right angle where it does not apply. The value 31° comes from halving, which is the centre-to-circumference rule, not the tangent–chord rule. The cue is 'alternate segment': the two angles are simply equal.

questions.stem: A network diagram is drawn to show the direct flights between six regional airports. In this diagram, what do the edges represent?
options: The direct flight routes joining pairs of airports
The airports being served by the airline
The physical ground distance between two airports, shown by the length of the line drawn
The number of passengers travelling between two airports each day
questions.explanation: In a network, vertices stand for the objects (here, the airports) and edges stand for the relationship between pairs of objects (here, a direct flight). The tempting wrong choice is that the length of a line shows the ground distance: in a network diagram the drawn length has no meaning at all, and only which vertices are joined matters. Read a network for its connections, not its picture geometry.

questions.stem: In a network, what is meant by the degree of a vertex?
options: The number of edges that meet at that vertex
The number of other vertices in the whole network
The smallest number of edges needed to travel from that vertex to any other
The number of vertices that are not joined to that vertex
questions.explanation: Degree simply counts the edge-ends meeting at a vertex, so a town with roads to three other towns has degree 3. The tempting wrong answer is the smallest number of edges needed to reach another vertex, which is a distance along a path, not a degree. Cue: degree is counted at the vertex itself, without travelling anywhere.

questions.stem: A network is described as connected. What does this tell you?
options: There is a path along edges from every vertex to every other vertex
Every vertex is joined directly by a single edge to every other vertex
Every vertex in the network has exactly the same degree
The network contains no loops and no repeated edges
questions.explanation: Connectedness only requires that you can get from any vertex to any other by travelling along one or more edges; the route may pass through several vertices. The tempting wrong answer, that every vertex is joined directly to every other, describes a complete network, which is a special case of a connected one. Cue: connected means reachable, not adjacent.

questions.stem: In a network of walking tracks between huts, the five huts have degrees 4, 3, 3, 2 and 2. How many tracks (edges) are in the network?
questions.explanation: Each edge has two ends, so it contributes 1 to the degree of each of the two vertices it joins; the sum of all degrees is therefore twice the number of edges. Here the degrees total 14, so there are 14 ÷ 2 = 7 tracks. The tempting wrong answer, 14, is the degree sum itself, forgetting that every edge has been counted twice.

questions.stem: A network diagram of a city's one-way street system shows an arrow drawn from vertex P to vertex Q. How should this be interpreted?
options: A vehicle can travel along that street in both directions between P and Q
P is the starting point of every journey that passes through the network
The street from P to Q is shorter than any other street leaving P
A vehicle can travel directly from P to Q, but not from Q to P along that street
questions.explanation: An arrow on an edge makes the network directed, and the direction of travel permitted is the direction the arrow points. The tempting wrong answer is that travel is possible both ways: that would be shown by an edge with no arrow, or by two arrows, one each way. Cue: arrows restrict direction, they say nothing about length or about where a journey begins.

questions.stem: A council wants to lay fibre cable so that all 9 community buildings can reach one another through the network. What is the smallest number of cables (edges) needed?
questions.explanation: To connect n vertices with no wasted edges you need a tree, which always has exactly n − 1 edges, so 9 buildings need 8 cables; adding a ninth would create a cycle that is not needed for connectedness. The tempting answer 36 is the number of cables if every pair were joined directly, which is far more than connectedness requires. Cue: connected means every building is reachable somehow, not joined to every other directly.

questions.stem: A network has edges A–B, B–C, A–C, D–E, E–F, D–F. Is it connected?
options: No, because there is no path from town A to town D
Yes, since every town has degree 2 and no town is isolated
Yes, because the number of edges equals the number of vertices
Yes, provided travel is allowed in both directions along every road
questions.explanation: A network is connected only when a path exists between every pair of vertices. Here A, B and C form one triangle and D, E and F form a separate triangle, with no edge joining the two groups, so the network has two components and is not connected. The tempting choice is the claim that it is connected because every town has degree 2 and none is isolated — but having a positive degree only guarantees a town is joined to something nearby, not that it can be reached from every other town. The cue: check whether you can travel from any one vertex to all the others, not just whether each vertex has edges.

questions.stem: A communications network has vertices P, Q, R, S, T and U, with links P–Q, Q–R, P–R, R–S, S–T, T–U and S–U. If exactly one link fails, which failure would leave the network disconnected?
options: T–U, because it is the last link listed in the network
R–S, because it is the only link joining the two triangles
P–Q, because P and Q would then have the lowest degrees
S–T, because T would then be cut off from the rest
questions.explanation: An edge whose removal disconnects a network is a bridge, and an edge is a bridge exactly when it lies on no cycle. P–Q, P–R and Q–R form one triangle and S–T, T–U and S–U form another, so each of those six edges sits on a cycle and can be lost without breaking connectedness; only R–S joins the two triangles. The most tempting wrong choice is S–T cutting off T, but T is still reachable through T–U and U–S. The cue: trace whether an alternative route exists around a cycle before deciding a link is critical.

questions.stem: The exterior angle theorem for a triangle states that an exterior angle is equal to:
options: the sum of the two interior opposite angles of the triangle
the interior angle adjacent to it at the same vertex
half the sum of the three interior angles of the triangle
the difference between the two interior opposite angles
questions.explanation: An exterior angle and its adjacent interior angle add to 180°, and the three interior angles also add to 180°, so the exterior angle must equal the other two interior angles added together. Saying it equals the adjacent interior angle is the common slip — those two angles are supplementary, and they are equal only in the special case where both are 90°. Look for the two angles 'far away' from the exterior angle: those are the ones you add.

questions.stem: Which piece of information is enough on its own to prove that two triangles are similar?
options: The two triangles have equal areas
One pair of corresponding angles is equal and one pair of corresponding sides is equal in length
Two pairs of corresponding angles are equal in size
Two pairs of corresponding sides are equal in length
questions.explanation: If two pairs of angles match, the third pair must match as well because the angle sum is 180°, so the triangles are equiangular and therefore similar. Two pairs of equal sides is tempting because it resembles a congruence test, but with no information about the angle between them or the third side the shapes can differ entirely. For similarity, chase angles or the ratios of all three sides — a mixture of one angle and one equal length controls nothing.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, AB = AC. Side BC is extended to D, and the exterior angle ACD measures 118°. What is the size of angle BAC?
questions.explanation: Angle ACB = 180° − 118° = 62°, and since AB = AC the base angles are equal, so angle ABC = 62° as well; the apex angle is 180° − 62° − 62° = 56°. Choosing 62° is the common error — that is a base angle, not the angle at A. Identify which angles sit opposite the equal sides first, then subtract from 180° for the remaining angle.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, D lies on AB and E lies on AC with DE parallel to BC. If AD = 4 cm, DB = 6 cm and AE = 6 cm, what is the length of EC?
questions.explanation: Because DE is parallel to BC, triangles ADE and ABC are equiangular and similar, giving AD/DB = AE/EC, so 4/6 = 6/EC and EC = 9 cm. Answering 6 cm assumes DE parallel to BC makes AE equal to EC, which would only happen if D were the midpoint of AB. Set up the ratio of matching parts on the same side of the triangle before substituting.

questions.stem: From an external point P, two tangents touch a circle with centre O at A and B. If angle APB = 40°, what is the size of angle AOB?
questions.explanation: A tangent meets the radius at the point of contact at 90°, so angles OAP and OBP are both 90°, and the angles of quadrilateral OAPB sum to 360°, giving angle AOB = 360° − 90° − 90° − 40° = 140°. Choosing 40° assumes the angle at the centre equals the angle at P, which is only true if all four angles were equal. The cue is the pair of right angles at the points of contact — they force the two remaining angles to be supplementary.

questions.stem: To prove that a quadrilateral ABCD with AB = CD and BC = DA must be a parallelogram, which deductive step should come first?
options: Draw diagonal AC and prove triangles ABC and CDA congruent using SAS
Assume AB is parallel to CD, then show the alternate angles are equal
Measure all four angles of ABCD and check that opposite angles are equal
Draw diagonal AC and prove triangles ABC and CDA congruent using SSS
questions.explanation: The diagonal AC is common to both triangles, so with AB = CD and BC = DA all three pairs of sides match and SSS applies; the equal alternate angles that follow then establish that the opposite sides are parallel. Using SAS is tempting but no pair of angles is given equal, so there is no included angle to use. Assuming AB is parallel to CD assumes the very thing being proved, which is not permitted in a deductive argument.

questions.stem: Two similar triangles have corresponding sides in the ratio 3 : 5. If the smaller triangle has an area of 18 cm², what is the area of the larger triangle?
questions.explanation: For similar figures, areas scale by the square of the side ratio, so the area factor is (5/3)² = 25/9 and 18 × 25/9 = 50 cm². Answering 30 cm² comes from multiplying by the linear factor 5/3, which scales lengths rather than areas. Whenever the question asks about area, square the length ratio before multiplying.

questions.stem: Two triangles are known to have all three pairs of corresponding angles equal. What can be deduced by valid reasoning?
options: They are similar, but not necessarily congruent
They are congruent, by the AAA congruence test
They are both similar and congruent, since equal angles force equal sides
They are neither similar nor congruent until a side length is known
questions.explanation: Equal corresponding angles fix the shape of a triangle but not its size, so the triangles are similar with sides in a constant ratio; an enlargement of a triangle keeps every angle the same. The option claiming congruence 'by the AAA congruence test' is the common trap — AAA is a similarity test, and there is no AAA congruence test, because a small and a large triangle can share all three angles. Remember: for congruence you always need at least one pair of matching sides (SSS, SAS, ASA or RHS).

questions.stem: A straight line touches a circle with centre O at the point T. Which statement is always true?
options: The line is perpendicular to every chord drawn from T
The line meets the circle again at the point opposite T
The radius OT is perpendicular to the line at T
The radius OT bisects the angle the line makes with the circle
questions.explanation: By the tangent–radius theorem, a tangent meets the radius drawn to the point of contact at 90°, which is why right angles appear in almost every tangent proof. The idea that OT 'bisects the angle the line makes with the circle' confuses this with the tangent–tangent result, where two tangents from an external point make equal angles with the line to the centre. The cue is the single point of contact: one tangent, one radius, one right angle.

questions.stem: A and B are fixed points on a circle. C and D are two other points on the circle, both on the same arc on one side of AB. What can be deduced about angle ACB and angle ADB?
options: They are equal, since they stand on the same arc AB
They add to 180°, since they stand on the same arc AB
Angle ACB is double angle ADB, since C is further from AB
They are equal only if CD passes through the centre
questions.explanation: Angles in the same segment are equal: each is half the angle AOB at the centre standing on the same arc, so both must be the same size. The option saying they add to 180° comes from the cyclic quadrilateral theorem, which applies to opposite angles of a quadrilateral inscribed in the circle, not to two angles on the same side of a chord. Check which side of the chord the vertices are on: same side means equal, opposite sides means supplementary.

questions.stem: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. Side AB is extended beyond B to a point E. The exterior angle CBE is equal to:
options: angle ADC, the interior opposite angle
angle DAB, the adjacent interior angle
questions.explanation: Angle ABC and angle ADC are opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral, so they add to 180°; angle CBE is also 180° minus angle ABC because ABE is a straight line, so angle CBE must equal angle ADC. The option '180° minus angle ADC' is the tempting one, but that expression equals angle ABC itself, not the exterior angle beside it. The shortcut to remember: the exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior angle at the opposite vertex.

questions.stem: In triangle PQR, M is the midpoint of PQ and N is the midpoint of PR. Side QR measures 14 cm. Using deductive reasoning about the similar triangles PMN and PQR, what can be concluded about MN?
options: MN = 28 cm and MN is parallel to QR
MN = 7 cm and MN is parallel to QR
MN = 7 cm and MN is perpendicular to QR
MN = 14 cm and MN is parallel to QR
questions.explanation: Triangles PMN and PQR share angle P and have PM : PQ = PN : PR = 1 : 2, so they are similar with scale factor ½; this makes MN half of QR, that is 7 cm, and makes angle PMN equal to angle PQR, which gives MN parallel to QR by corresponding angles. The version with MN = 7 cm but perpendicular to QR gets the length right and then invents a right angle that no theorem supplies. The midsegment result is always half as long and parallel, never perpendicular.

questions.stem: AB is a chord of a circle with centre O, and angle OAB = 34°. What is the size of angle AOB?
questions.explanation: OA and OB are both radii, so triangle OAB is isosceles and angle OBA also equals 34°; the angle sum of the triangle then gives angle AOB = 180° − 34° − 34° = 112°. The answer 68° comes from applying the angle-at-the-centre theorem (doubling 34°), but that theorem needs the vertex of the 34° angle on the circumference standing on chord AB, not at A itself with the radius. Whenever two radii and a chord form a triangle, start by writing 'isosceles, base angles equal'.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC the angle at C is 90°, and CD is the altitude drawn from C perpendicular to the hypotenuse AB, with D on AB. If AD = 4 cm and DB = 9 cm, what is the length of CD?
questions.explanation: Triangles ACD and CBD are both similar to triangle ABC (shared angles and right angles), so AD : CD = CD : DB, giving CD² = 4 × 9 = 36 and CD = 6 cm. The answer 6.5 cm comes from averaging 4 and 9, which would only be the length of a median-type segment, not the geometric mean that similarity produces. The cue is the proportion CD/AD = DB/CD: the altitude is the geometric mean of the two hypotenuse pieces, so multiply then take the square root.

questions.stem: In a deductive geometric proof, a statement accepted as true without proof and used as a starting point is called:
questions.explanation: Deductive proof starts from axioms (statements assumed true), then uses logical steps to establish theorems. Calling it a theorem is tempting, but a theorem is the result you prove using axioms and earlier theorems, not the unproved starting point. A converse swaps the 'if' and 'then' parts of a statement, and a corollary is a quick consequence of a theorem already proved.

questions.stem: Two triangles have two pairs of corresponding sides equal and the pair of angles between those sides equal. Which congruence test does this describe?
questions.explanation: When two sides and the included angle match, the triangles are congruent by SAS, because the third side is fixed by those two sides and the angle between them. SSS is tempting but requires all three pairs of sides to be known equal, and here only two are given. AAS needs two angles and a side, while RHS applies only to right-angled triangles with hypotenuse and one other side equal.

questions.stem: In a circle with centre O, a chord AB is not a diameter and M is the midpoint of AB. Which conclusion follows from the standard chord theorem?
options: OM is parallel to the tangent at A
OM is equal in length to AM
questions.explanation: The line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to that chord, since triangles OAM and OBM are congruent by SSS and the two angles at M are equal and supplementary. Saying OM equals AM is wrong: those lengths depend on how far the chord sits from the centre and are only equal in one special case, not in general. The correct cue is that 'centre to midpoint of chord' always signals a right angle.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, angle B = 90°. D is a point on AB and E is a point on BC, and DE is drawn. Given BD = 3 cm, BE = 4 cm, BA = 9 cm and BC = 12 cm, what can be deduced about DE and AC?
options: DE and AC cannot be compared without knowing angle A
DE is parallel to AC, and AC = 3 × DE
DE is perpendicular to AC, and AC = 3 × DE
DE is parallel to AC, and AC = 9 × DE
questions.explanation: Triangles DBE and ABC share the angle at B and have BD/BA = BE/BC = 1/3, so they are similar by SAS similarity; corresponding angles BDE and BAC are therefore equal, making DE parallel to AC, and every side of ABC is 3 times the matching side of DBE. Choosing AC = 9 × DE confuses the area ratio 3² = 9 with the length ratio 3. Remember that the scale factor multiplies lengths, while its square multiplies areas.

questions.stem: In a circle, chord AB subtends an angle of 40° at point C on the major arc. Point D also lies on the major arc, and E lies on the minor arc. Which deduction is correct?
questions.explanation: Angles in the same segment are equal, so D on the major arc gives angle ADB = 40°; since ADBE (in some order) forms a cyclic quadrilateral, the angle at E on the opposite arc is supplementary, giving 180° − 40° = 140°. Saying both angles are 40° applies the same-segment rule to a point in the opposite segment, where the supplementary rule takes over. The cue is which side of the chord the point lies on: same side means equal, opposite side means adding to 180°.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, point D lies on AB and point E lies on AC. It is given that angle ADE = angle ACB, AD = 4 cm, AE = 5 cm and AC = 10 cm. Using deductive reasoning about the similar triangles, what is the length of AB?
questions.explanation: Angle A is common to both triangles and angle ADE = angle ACB is given, so triangle ADE is similar to triangle ACB by AA — note the correspondence A↔A, D↔C, E↔B. Matching sides therefore gives AD/AC = AE/AB, so 4/10 = 5/AB and AB = 5 × 10 ÷ 4 = 12.5 cm. The answer 8 cm comes from pairing D with B and E with C (writing AD/AB = AE/AC), which ignores the given equal angles that fix the correspondence. The cue: write the vertices of the two triangles in matching order first, letting the equal angles decide which vertex pairs with which, then form the ratios.

questions.stem: In a network diagram, a loop is:
options: an edge that joins two different vertices
a route that starts and finishes at the same vertex after visiting others
a vertex that has no edges connected to it
an edge that joins a vertex to itself
questions.explanation: A loop is a single edge whose two ends are the same vertex, so it shows a connection from something back to itself (for example a webpage linking to itself). The option describing a route that starts and finishes at the same vertex is really a closed walk or cycle, which uses several edges rather than one edge at a single vertex. The cue is that a loop is one edge, drawn as a small circle at one vertex, not a journey through the network.

questions.stem: For any network diagram, the sum of the degrees of all the vertices is always:
options: equal to the number of edges
equal to the number of vertices
questions.explanation: Each edge has two ends, and each end adds 1 to the degree of the vertex it meets, so every edge contributes 2 to the total of all degrees. The tempting choice 'equal to the number of edges' forgets that an edge is counted at both of the vertices it joins. Check with a simple example: a triangle has 3 edges and degrees 2, 2, 2, giving a total of 6 = 2 × 3.

questions.stem: Five computers in an office are each connected directly to every one of the other computers. How many edges does the network diagram have?
questions.explanation: Each of the 5 computers has degree 4, so the degrees total 5 × 4 = 20, and since every edge is counted twice the number of edges is 20 ÷ 2 = 10. Choosing 20 is the common slip of stopping at the degree total instead of halving it. Whenever you add degrees, remember to divide by 2 to get edges.

questions.stem: A network diagram of walking tracks shows 9 huts, which form three separate groups; there are tracks within each group but none between the groups. What is the smallest number of new tracks needed so that every hut can be reached from every other hut?
questions.explanation: Each new track can join two separate groups into one, so joining three groups into a single connected network needs 3 − 1 = 2 new tracks. Choosing 3 assumes one new track per group, but the last group is already linked once the first two joins are made. The rule to remember is: new edges needed = number of separate parts − 1.

questions.stem: A rail network has stations A, B, C, D, E and F, with direct lines A–B, B–C, A–C, C–D, C–E, D–E, D–F and E–F. If one station is closed and all lines through it are shut, which closure would leave the remaining stations disconnected from one another?
questions.explanation: Station C is the only link between the pair A, B and the group D, E, F, so closing C leaves A–B cut off from D–E–F. Closing D looks tempting because D has degree 3, but E still joins to C and F, so the rest stays connected; the same is true for E. High degree does not make a vertex critical — what matters is whether it is the only bridge between two parts of the network.

questions.stem: What do the angles of a triangle add to?
questions.explanation: Any triangle's interior angles total 180 degrees. 360 is the total for a quadrilateral, which is the usual confusion.
questions.teaching:
This is one of the most useful facts in geometry because it lets you find a missing angle from the other two by subtraction.

The result holds for every triangle without exception — tall, thin, obtuse, right-angled. You can see why by tearing the three corners off a paper triangle and placing them together: they form a straight line. That gives the total directly. Quadrilaterals total twice as much, and the general rule for any polygon is 180 multiplied by two fewer than the number of sides. Mixing up the triangle total with the quadrilateral total is the usual slip.

questions.stem: What does 'congruent' mean for two shapes?
questions.explanation: Congruent shapes are identical — you could lay one exactly over the other, possibly after turning or flipping it. Same shape at a different size is similar, not congruent.
questions.teaching:
Two words get used for shapes that resemble each other, and they mean genuinely different things.

One means identical in every measurement: lay one over the other and they coincide exactly. You are allowed to slide, turn or flip a shape to line it up, since those moves change position rather than dimensions. The other word is looser — the angles all match while the sides sit in a fixed ratio, so one shape is a scaled photocopy of the other. Every pair of the first kind also satisfies the second, with a scale factor of one; the reverse does not hold. Scale models and enlargements on a map are the second relationship, never the first.

questions.stem: What does 'similar' mean for two shapes?
options: Same shape and exactly the same size
questions.explanation: Similar shapes have equal angles and sides in the same ratio, so one is a scaled copy of the other. Congruent is the special case where the scale factor happens to be 1.
questions.teaching:
Two words describe shapes that resemble one another, and the difference is whether size is included.

One requires everything to match exactly — same angles, same side lengths — so one shape could be laid over the other and coincide. The other requires only that the angles match and the sides sit in a constant ratio, so one is a scaled version of the other. That scaling is what makes maps, scale models and photograph enlargements work, and it is what lets you find an unknown side by setting up a ratio. Shapes matching exactly are a special case of the looser relationship, with a scale factor of one.

questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle, what is the sine ratio?
questions.explanation: SOH tells you sine is opposite over hypotenuse. Adjacent over hypotenuse is cosine, so the first two options are the pair most often swapped.
questions.teaching:
Trigonometry rests on one observation: in a right-angled triangle, once you fix one of the other angles the shape is fixed too. Make the triangle bigger and every side grows in the same proportion, so the ratio between any two sides depends only on the angle — which means it can be tabulated and looked up.

Three of those ratios get names, and the labelling is what students get wrong. The longest side, facing the right angle, is the hypotenuse and never moves. The other two are named relative to whichever angle you are working from: one sits directly across from it, the other lies alongside it. Switch to the other angle and those two swap roles. SOH CAH TOA is the standard memory aid — but label the triangle first, then choose.

questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle, what is the cosine ratio?
questions.explanation: CAH gives cosine as adjacent over hypotenuse. Which side counts as adjacent depends on the angle you are working from, so label the triangle before choosing a ratio.
questions.teaching:
The three trigonometric ratios each pair two of the triangle's three sides, and SOH CAH TOA lists them in order.

The hypotenuse is fixed — always the side facing the right angle, always the longest. The other two are named relative to the angle you are working from: one directly across from it, one alongside it. Read the memory aid in three-letter blocks and each block gives you a ratio: the first letter is the function, the second is the top of the fraction, the third is the bottom. Label your triangle before choosing, because switching to the other angle swaps which side is which.

questions.stem: How many degrees are in a full turn?
questions.explanation: A full turn is 360 degrees, half a turn 180 and a quarter turn 90. Answering 180 describes a straight line rather than a complete revolution.
questions.teaching:
Angle facts build on one another, so it is worth anchoring them to a complete rotation and working down.

A complete rotation is divided into 360 parts, a number inherited from Babylonian astronomy and convenient because it divides evenly so many ways. Half of that is a straight line, and a quarter is a right angle. From those three you can derive most of what you need: angles on a straight line sum to the half-turn figure, angles round a point sum to the full one, and a triangle's angles sum to the half-turn figure too. Confusing the straight-line value with the full rotation is the usual error.

questions.stem: What is the transformation that turns a shape called?
questions.explanation: A rotation turns a shape about a fixed point. A translation slides it and a reflection flips it, so all three move the shape without changing its size.
questions.teaching:
Four transformations are taught together, and each does one specific thing to a shape.

One slides it without changing its orientation. One flips it over a line, producing a mirror image. One turns it about a fixed point through a given angle. And one changes its size by a scale factor. The first three preserve size and shape entirely, so the result is congruent to the original; only the fourth changes size, producing a similar shape rather than an identical one. Sorting them by what stays the same is the quickest way to keep the four names straight.

questions.stem: What does the tangent ratio equal?
questions.explanation: TOA gives tangent as opposite over adjacent — the only one of the three ratios that leaves the hypotenuse out entirely, which makes it easy to spot.
questions.teaching:
Of the three trigonometric ratios, this one has a feature that makes it easy to identify: it is the only one that does not involve the hypotenuse.

Both of the others compare a side to the hypotenuse. This one compares the two shorter sides to each other, which is exactly why it is the ratio you want when you know nothing about the longest side — working out a tree's height from your distance to it and the angle you look up, for instance. In SOH CAH TOA, it is the last block. Sorting by whether the hypotenuse appears cuts the three options down to one immediately.
